opus-5.5.text:
It's an appealing idea, and it's one I've thought about quite a bit, partly because it's so intuitive. Children don't start out hearing long sentences with nested relative clauses; the speech directed at them tends to be shorter and simpler. So it's natural to ask whether a model would learn syntax more efficiently, or generalize more like humans do, if we structured its input that way.

I'd separate two questions, though. One is engineering: does a curriculum make training faster or cheaper, or improve performance on some benchmark? The other is scientific: does it change the inductive biases the model ends up with, for example whether it generalizes hierarchically rather than relying on linear-order heuristics? That second question is the one I care more about, because the core puzzle in language acquisition isn't how quickly you learn but which generalization you settle on when the data is ambiguous.

My read on the evidence is that the results have been mixed and often fairly modest. Curriculum learning in machine learning generally has a long history of being promising in principle and less consistent in practice. With large models and lots of data, the order of presentation often seems to matter less than you'd expect; the model eventually sees everything, and the end state isn't dramatically different. There are also cases where starting simple can hurt, if the model latches onto shortcuts that work for simple sentences but don't extend to complex ones.

There's also the question of what "simple" means. Sentence length is an easy proxy, but it isn't the same as syntactic complexity, and child-directed speech isn't simple in a uniform way; it has plenty of questions and fragments, for instance. So if we want to make claims about human learning, we need to be careful that our curriculum actually resembles what children experience rather than an idealized version of it.

So I see curricula as a useful experimental tool. They let us manipulate the input and ask what really drives syntactic generalization. But I'm skeptical that ordering alone is the missing ingredient that makes models learn like children. It's more likely that the amount of data, the architecture's inductive biases, and perhaps the fact that children learn language grounded in interaction and meaning all matter a lot more. The interesting work is in teasing those factors apart.

r001.rationale: The response links children’s exposure to shorter, simpler speech with the idea of structuring a model’s input from simple sentences to more complex ones.

fable-5.1.text:
Tal Linzen: It's an appealing idea, and it has a long history in cognitive science, so I want to take it seriously before I say where I'm skeptical.

The intuition comes from Elman's "starting small" work in the early nineties. He trained a recurrent network on sentences with long-distance dependencies, and it struggled until he either fed it simple sentences first or started it out with a very limited memory window. The story was that a constrained learner is forced to pick up the local regularities, like subject-verb agreement in short clauses, and only then can it build up to the embedded cases. That maps nicely onto what children seem to do, where their early productions are short and gradually become more complex.

The problem is that the result turned out to be fragile. Rohde and Plaut went back and showed that with somewhat different training details, starting with the full complexity was as good or better. So even in the small-network era, it was never clear that curricula were doing the work the theory said they were.

With modern language models, my read is that the effect is mostly washed out. These models are trained on so much data that whatever benefit you get from ordering it is swamped by the sheer volume, and in a lot of experiments, including some from the BabyLM community that tried explicitly to use developmentally ordered data, curricula either didn't help or helped marginally and inconsistently. The models seem to figure out that agreement or relative clause attachment is a hierarchical phenomenon whether or not you spoon-feed them the easy cases first. Where they fail, and they do still fail on things like agreement across attractors or center embedding, it hasn't been obvious that ordering the data is the lever that fixes it.

There's also a conceptual issue I care about more, which is that "simple to complex" presupposes we know what the right notion of complexity is. Sentence length is a crude proxy. A short sentence can involve a nontrivial dependency, and a long sentence can be a list of coordinated noun phrases. If you want the curriculum to teach syntax, you need to order by syntactic structure, which means you've already committed to a particular grammar in designing the data. At that point you're partly building in what you're hoping the model will discover, and the scientific question gets muddier.

What I do find interesting is the flip side: using models as a testbed for these cognitive hypotheses rather than as the beneficiaries of them. If a curriculum helps a model generalize hierarchically from an amount of data that's in the vicinity of what a child sees, that tells us something about whether input ordering could plausibly be part of the human story. If it doesn't help even at that scale, that's evidence too. So I think of curricula less as an engineering trick for better language models and more as an experimental manipulation that lets us ask what kind of inductive bias is actually necessary to learn syntax from data.

r001.rationale: The response connects training on simple sentences before more complex structures to children’s progression from short early productions to increasingly complex language.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s an interesting idea, but I would separate two questions. One is whether a curriculum helps a model learn syntax more effectively, and the other is whether that curriculum resembles what children actually experience. Those aren’t necessarily the same thing. Children don’t get a neatly ordered sequence of sentences that starts with the simplest structures and gradually introduces more complicated ones.

From the modeling perspective, the important question is what the model generalizes to. If you start with simple sentences and then introduce more complex ones, does it learn something about hierarchical structure that it can apply to constructions it hasn’t seen? Or does it just become better at the particular patterns in the curriculum?

I’d want to compare that with a model trained on exactly the same data in a different order. And I’d be especially interested in whether the curriculum helps when the amount of training data is limited. That would tell us something useful about how to make learning more efficient, even if it didn’t turn out to be a good account of how children acquire language.

r001.rationale: The response directly compares a simple-to-complex sentence curriculum with what children experience during language learning, noting that children do not receive a neatly ordered progression.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it’s a reasonable idea to explore. There’s an intuition that you should learn simple sentences first and then build up to more complex ones. But I wouldn’t take for granted that this is how children learn, or that the order that seems natural to us is necessarily the best order for a language model.

One question is what you mean by complexity. A sentence can be long but syntactically straightforward, or short and still involve a difficult dependency. So you’d want to be quite precise about what the curriculum is manipulating.

For me, the interesting test would be whether the model learns something that generalizes. If you train it on simpler structures, does that help it handle new combinations of those structures, or dependencies that are longer than anything it’s seen? You’d also want to compare it with a model trained on exactly the same data in a different order. That would help establish whether the curriculum itself is doing useful work.

r001.rationale: The response connects a language-model curriculum that starts with simple sentences and builds toward complex ones to the intuition about human learning, while noting that children may not actually learn in that order.
